title: Do You Know This Blizzard of Winter Words?
main_content:
Today, we talk about expressions that come from extreme winter weather.

Winters in the northern United States are cold and snowy. Sometimes, the snows come with extremely strong winds. These snow storms are called blizzards. 

The dictionary Etymology Online says “blizzard” came to mean a severe snowstorm during the late 1800s. Before then, the word “blizzard” had nothing to do with snow. It had several other meanings. One was a sharp blow. Another meaning was a gunshot. And blizzard was also defined as a most extreme statement or event.

These days, we do not use “blizzard” to mean any of those things. Blizzard is only used to mean an extreme snow storm.

Even though blizzards can be dangerous, some people still enjoy the excitement caused by this extreme weather.

But no one likes to be snowed.

Snow as a verb means to tell someone many pleasant but false statements.

questions.question: When did the word “blizzard” come to mean “a severe snowstorm”?
options: Around the turn of the century

questions.question: What does “to snow (someone)” mean?
options: To deceive someone with pleasant lies
To confuse someone with complicated instructions
questions.answer: To deceive someone with pleasant lies

questions.question: What were the other meanings of the word “blizzard”?
options: An extreme statement or event, a sharp blow, a gunshot
An indication of a severe weather forecast
questions.answer: An extreme statement or event, a sharp blow, a gunshot
